ideas.title: Red Bull Got Sued Because It Didn't Give Wings
ideas.story: Owner doc concept 1 (5-7 min). 2013 class action (Careathers v. Red Bull) attacked the performance claims, not literal wings; an 8.4 oz can has about as much caffeine as a cup of coffee; Red Bull settled for $13 million: $10 cash or $15 of products to anyone who bought a can 2002-2014, no receipt needed; claim site was flooded. Arc: hook headline, the slogan that built the empire, coffee comparison, the settlement frenzy, what changed. Owner's script figures (caffeine mg, 27 g sugar, 'crashed in 48 hours', dates) are unverified: fact-check each with 2 sources.

ideas.title: The Maths Retiree Who Cracked a State Lottery (Cash WinFall)
ideas.story: Owner doc concept 3 (6-8 min). Jerry Selbee noticed Michigan's Cash WinFall roll-down: when the jackpot hit $5 million unwon, the money rolled down to 3/4/5-number matches, making a $1 ticket worth more than $1. His syndicate (with wife Marge) later played the Massachusetts version for years and won tens of millions legally; Boston Globe story 2011; state investigation found no laws broken; game ended. Owner's figures ($5.50 per ticket, $26M, 9 years, 14-hour days, GS Investment Strategies) need 2-source checks.

ideas.title: The Real Estate Empire Hidden Inside McDonald's
ideas.story: Owner doc concept 4 (6-8 min). Harry Sonneborn, McDonald's first CFO, said they are in the real estate business; Franchise Realty Corporation bought land and leased it back to franchisees (rent as higher of base or percentage of sales); owning the land gave Kroc steady cash flow and leverage. Owner's figures (1.9% royalty, 85% owned, $40B+, 'top five private real estate owners') are unverified: fact-check each, drop what fails.

ideas.title: How Pepsi Accidentally Promised a Harrier Jump Jet
ideas.story: Owner doc concept 2 (7-9 min). 1996 Pepsi Stuff ad offered a Harrier jet for 7,000,000 points; John Leonard saw points could be bought for 10 cents each ($700,000), raised investors, sent the check; Pepsi refused; Leonard v. PepsiCo, Judge Kimba Wood ruled for Pepsi in 1999 (no reasonable person); Pepsi later changed the ad to 700,000,000 points. We already made a Short on this (005): the long must add new depth and re-verify every number from the owner's script (dates, investor count, Pentagon statement).

Sneaky Deals — Long-Form Content Production Guide

Concept 1: Red Bull Sued Because Drink Did Not Give Wings

Core Theme: False advertising, corporate settlements, marketing blunders.

Target Run Time: 5–7 minutes

The Premise: In 2013, a consumer filed a class-action lawsuit against Red Bull in federal court. Rather than expecting literal wings, the suit attacked Red Bull’s claims of superior physical and mental enhancement, proving an 8.4 oz can had no more caffeine than ordinary coffee. Red Bull settled for $13 million, offering $10 cash or free products to anyone who bought a can between 2002 and 2014 without requiring a receipt.

Narrative Arc:

Hook (0:00–0:45): Highlight the ridiculous headline, then pivot to the real embarrassing reason Red Bull settled.

Chapter 1: The Slogan That Built an Empire (0:45–2:00): How the extreme sports image and the "wings" slogan justified a premium price tag.

Chapter 2: The Coffee Comparison (2:00–3:30): Breaking down the science—comparing 80mg caffeine in a $3 can to a 50¢ diner coffee.

Chapter 3: The $13M Internet Frenzy (3:30–5:00): Millions flooded the claim website, crashing the servers to get a $10 payout or two free cans.

Outro (5:00–5:45): What changed for energy drink labels and a community prompt: "Did you claim your $10 back then?"

Concept 2: How Pepsi Accidentally Promised a Harrier Jump Jet

Core Theme: Marketing promotions gone wrong, contractual loopholes, high-stakes legal battles.

Target Run Time: 7–9 minutes

The Premise: During the 1996 "Pepsi Stuff" promotion, a commercial jokingly displayed a $30 million military Harrier Jump Jet for 7,000,000 Pepsi points. A 21-year-old business student discovered a rule in the fine print: points could be purchased for 10 cents each. He raised $700,000 from investors, sent Pepsi a check with 15 original points, and demanded the jet—leading to a landmark federal court showdown.

Narrative Arc:

Hook (0:00–1:00): Show the original 1996 commercial offering a military combat jet, then reveal someone actually called their bluff.

Chapter 1: The Pepsi Stuff Phenomenon (1:00–2:30): The 1990s cola wars, promotional craze, and the fine print that opened the door.

Chapter 2: The Investor Syndicate (2:30–4:30): How John Leonard secured $700,000 to buy points directly and mailed the official request.

Chapter 3: The Pentagon & The Courtroom (4:30–7:00): Pepsi's panic, Pentagon intervention (demilitarizing combat aircraft), and the judge's ruling on whether a commercial is a binding contract.

Outro (7:00–8:00): How Pepsi updated the ad to 700,000,000 points and what it taught corporate legal teams forever.

Concept 3: The Mathematics Professor Who Cracked the State Lottery

Core Theme: System loopholes, underdog stories, mathematical exploitation.

Target Run Time: 6–8 minutes

The Premise: In 2003, retired mathematician Jerry Selbee noticed a flaw in Michigan’s "Cash WinFall" lottery. Due to a unique "roll-down" rule, whenever the jackpot hit $5 million without a winner, the prize money rolled down to lower-tier matches (four- and three-number winners). Selbee calculated that when a roll-down occurred, each $1 ticket was statistically worth over $5. Over nine years, his small syndicate legally won over $26 million.

Narrative Arc:

Hook (0:00–0:45): Contrast typical lottery odds with someone who cracked a guaranteed profit formula in under three minutes of basic math.

Chapter 1: The Roll-Down Flaw (0:45–2:15): Explain the Cash WinFall mechanism simply with clean visual aids showing the payout shift.

Chapter 2: The Bulk Ticket Operation (2:15–4:30): The logistics—standing at convenience store terminals printing hundreds of thousands of tickets for days at a time.

Chapter 3: The State Investigation (4:30–6:30): Lottery officials notice the massive volume, launch a fraud investigation, and discover everything was 100% legal.

Outro (6:30–7:30): The shutdown of the game and how the loophole was never repeated.

Concept 4: The Real Estate Empire Hidden Inside a Fast Food Giant

Core Theme: Covert business models, corporate strategy, massive real estate holdings.

Target Run Time: 6–8 minutes

The Premise: While McDonald's appears to sell burgers and fries, its real business is prime commercial real estate. Former CFO Harry Sonneborn famously stated: "We are not technically in the food business. We are in the real estate business." By purchasing the land under franchisees' locations and collecting escalating rent, the company built one of the world's most resilient real estate portfolios (worth tens of billions).

Narrative Arc:

Hook (0:00–0:45): Quote Harry Sonneborn's famous line and contrast store revenue with property ownership.

Chapter 1: The Franchisee Crisis (0:45–2:30): Ray Kroc's early struggle to stay profitable while franchisees made all the money.

Chapter 2: The Sonneborn Model (2:30–4:30): How buying the physical dirt and leasing it back created guaranteed cash flow regardless of burger sales.

Chapter 3: Surviving Economic Crashes (4:30–6:00): How property ownership shielded the brand while traditional restaurant competitors folded.

Outro (6:00–7:00): Why this model makes the company virtually untouchable today, tied into the channel's recurring theme of hidden deals.
